zh_summary: $NBIS는 약속된 ARR의 8.1배로 거래되며, $IREN의 5.1배, $CRWV의 2.5배와 비교된다. CoreWeave는 약 350억 달러 약속, Nebius 약 100억 달러, IREN 약 40억 달러다. Nebius는 활성 약 250 MW에 대해 3.5 GW 계약이 있으며, 그 미래 용량의 약 75%가 소유 부지에 있어 잠재적 성장의 대부분이 아직 앞에 있다. Nebius는 MW당 약 1300만 달러 수익을 창출하며 CoreWeave의 약 1100만 달러와 비교되며, 추론 소프트웨어 확장으로 프리미엄을 설명하고 CoreWeave의 더 무거운 부채와 함께한다.
text:
$NBIS trades at 8.1x committed ARR versus 5.1x for $IREN and 2.5x for $CRWV even though CoreWeave has ~$35B committed compared with Nebius at ~$10B and IREN at ~$4B.

Essentially the difference is Nebius has only ~250 MW active against 3.5 GW contracted with ~75% of that future capacity on owned sites meaning most of its potential growth is still ahead.

Nebius also generates~$13M in revenue per MW versus ~$11M for CoreWeave as inference software expands helping explain the premium alongside CoreWeave’s heavier debt.

John, you are almost always an admirably clear thinker. But you endorse a common fallacy when you make this argument: "Higher rates hurt supply-side solutions in housing, energy, autos, and other capital intensive industries"

The issue is that much more demand is reduced before any supply is reduced. For example, higher interest rates might cut $100 of upfront spending and result in $5/yr less in supply starting 3 years from now. That is deflationary.

You can also think of your argument in reverse. If the government made a big increase in infrastructure investment or businesses suddenly decided to invest more in autos we would expect that to put upward pressure on inflation not downward pressure.

name: John_Hempton
zh_summary: 이것은 금융 기관이 어떻게 파산하는지에 대한 놀라운 오해다. 자산이 나빠질 때가 아니라 자금 조달이 불가능해질 때 파산한다. 물론 자금 시장이 더 이상 자산을 신뢰하지 않을 때 자금 조달이 나빠진다. 그들은 원하는 만큼 연장하고 가장할 수 있다. 하지만 자산 담보 어음 시장이 자산을 신뢰하지 않으면 도움이 되지 않는다. 이 경우 신뢰가 사라진 가능성이 매우 높다.
text:
This is a spectacular misunderstanding of how financial institutions go bankrupt.

They go bankrupt not when the assets go bad but when their funding becomes impossible.

Sure the funding goes bad when the funding market no longer trusts the assets.

They can extend and pretend as long as they like. But it won't help them if say the asset backed paper market doesn't trust the assets.

In this case there is a very high chance that trust has gone away.

text:
If high-quality bonds protect against one kind of crash but not the other, what else belongs in the portfolio? Many products are sold as crash protection. The fairest test is to see what each did in the two most recent, very different stress years.

The chart repays careful reading.

* Stocks of every kind fell in both years. International stocks and real estate did not protect U.S. investors in either crash. Their case rests on long-run diversification, not crash protection. Within U.S. stocks, value shares held up far better than growth shares in 2022, but not in 2008.

* Long-term Treasuries and commodities are mirror images. Each saved the portfolio in one year and hurt it badly in the other. Holding a modest amount of both is a hedge against not knowing which engine will run.

* Gold roughly held its value in both years. It pays no income, and it can fall sharply in other periods, as it did in the early 1980s and in 2013. It is a store of value in a crisis, not a growth engine. 

*Managed futures gained in both years. These funds follow price trends across stocks, bonds, currencies, and commodities, going long or short. They tend to do well in extended declines of any kind. They can also lag for years in calm, trendless markets, and their fees are higher than index funds’.

*Treasury bills gained in both years. Its cost is low returns in good times.

And I think Bill Ackman has the better map of how this ends.

Burry's Oct 11 note is clear: he sold the common, bought junior preferred, and flagged a Treasury conversion of the senior preferred (SPS) into common — dilution of 90%+.

That risk is real on paper.
I just don't think it's the base case the Trump team is trying to deliver.

Here's why I side with Ackman:

1. The SPS has already been paid — economically.

Fannie and Freddie drew about $193B from Treasury after 2008.
They have since returned about $301B in dividends.

Ackman's point is simple: treat the senior preferred as repaid, don't invent a brand-new dilution event to wipe out private common holders.

2. Ackman's path preserves the common.

His three-step plan:
→ Treasury / FHFA amend the PSPA so the SPS is treated as satisfied
→ Treasury exercises its warrants for ~79.9% of the common
→ Relist on the NYSE while conservatorship continues

Government control stays.
Mortgage markets aren't disrupted.
Existing common isn't vaporized by a 90% conversion.

That is "walk before you run," not "convert and crush."
